claim: BEST1 plays an indispensable role in generating Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in human RPE cells.
source: Previously, we showed that BEST1 plays an indispensable role in generating Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in human RPE cells, and the deficiency of BEST1 function in patient-derived RPE is rescuable by gene augmentation (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Li et al., 2017) and by experimental data in the current manuscript showing abolished currents in BEST1-/- cells.

claim: The deficiency of BEST1 function in patient-derived RPE is rescuable by gene augmentation.
source: Previously, we showed that BEST1 plays an indispensable role in generating Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in human RPE cells, and the deficiency of BEST1 function in patient-derived RPE is rescuable by gene augmentation (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Li et al., 2017).

claim: BEST1 patient-derived loss-of-function and gain-of-function mutations require different mutant to wild-type molecule ratios for phenotypic manifestation.
source: Here, we report that BEST1 patient-derived loss-of-function and gain-of-function mutations require different mutant to wild-type (WT) molecule ratios for phenotypic manifestation, underlying their distinct epigenetic requirements in bestrophinopathy development, and suggesting that some of the previously classified autosomal dominant mutations actually behave in a dominant-negative manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different ratios required for loss-of-function vs gain-of-function mutations to exhibit phenotypes.

claim: Some of the previously classified autosomal dominant BEST1 mutations actually behave in a dominant-negative manner.
source: Here, we report that BEST1 patient-derived loss-of-function and gain-of-function mutations require different mutant to wild-type (WT) molecule ratios for phenotypic manifestation, underlying their distinct epigenetic requirements in bestrophinopathy development, and suggesting that some of the previously classified autosomal dominant mutations actually behave in a dominant-negative manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations require a 4:1 ratio to exhibit phenotype.

claim: The strong dominant effect of BEST1 gain-of-function mutations prohibits the restoration of BEST1-dependent Cl- currents in RPE cells by gene augmentation.
source: Importantly, the strong dominant effect of BEST1 gain-of-function mutations prohibits the restoration of BEST1-dependent Cl- currents in RPE cells by gene augmentation, in contrast to the efficient rescue of loss-of-function mutations via the same approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that gene augmentation alone cannot rescue gain-of-function mutations in hPSC-RPE cells.

claim: Loss-of-function BEST1 mutations are efficiently rescued by gene augmentation.
source: Importantly, the strong dominant effect of BEST1 gain-of-function mutations prohibits the restoration of BEST1-dependent Cl- currents in RPE cells by gene augmentation, in contrast to the efficient rescue of loss-of-function mutations via the same approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: Gain-of-function BEST1 mutations are rescuable by a combination of gene augmentation with CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of endogenous BEST1 expression.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that gain-of-function mutations are rescuable by a combination of gene augmentation with CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of endogenous BEST1 expression, providing a universal treatment strategy for all bestrophinopathy patients regardless of their mutation types.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of gain-of-function mutations using BVSi silencing plus wobble WT BEST1 augmentation.

claim: Over 250 distinct BEST1 mutations have been identified from bestrophinopathy patients.
source: To date, over 250 distinct BEST1 mutations have been identified from bestrophinopathy patients, but their pathological mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The majority of BEST1 mutations are autosomal dominant.
source: The majority of the BEST1 mutations are autosomal dominant, whereas the autosomal recessive ones are specifically linked to ARB (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Johnson et al., 2017).

claim: Autosomal recessive BEST1 mutations are specifically linked to ARB.
source: The majority of the BEST1 mutations are autosomal dominant, whereas the autosomal recessive ones are specifically linked to ARB (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Johnson et al., 2017).

claim: BEST1 is a Ca2+-activated Cl- channel predominantly expressed in retinal pigment epithelium.
source: Functionally, bestrophin-1 (BEST1), the protein encoded by BEST1, is a Ca2+-activated Cl- channel (CaCC) predominantly expressed in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Marmorstein et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Marmorstein et al., 2000).

claim: Bestrophinopathy patient-derived RPE cells exhibit abnormal Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents.
source: Bestrophinopathy patient-derived RPE cells exhibit abnormal Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents, underscoring the indispensable role of BEST1 as a CaCC in RPE (Li et al., 2017), although the contribution of other candidate CaCCs cannot be excluded.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Li et al., 2017).

claim: BEST1 is a highly conserved pentamer with a flower vase-shaped ion conducting pathway.
source: Structurally, while the human BEST1 structure has not been solved, high-resolution structures of three homologs from Klebsiella pneumoniae (KpBEST), chicken (cBEST1), and bovine (bBEST2) indicate that the channel is a highly conserved pentamer with a flower vase-shaped ion conducting pathway (Yang et al., 2014a; Kane Dickson et al., 2014; Owji et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies (Yang et al., 2014a; Kane Dickson et al., 2014; Owji et al., 2020).

claim: The vast majority of tested patient-derived BEST1 mutations exhibited a loss-of-function phenotype.
source: The vast majority of the tested patient-derived mutations exhibited a loss-of-function phenotype, as the Cl- currents mediated by the mutant channels are significantly reduced compared to the wild-type (WT) BEST1 (Li et al., 2017; Hartzell et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2014; Ji et al., 2019a; Ji et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Several BEST1 gain-of-function mutations enhance channel activity when transiently expressed in HEK293 cells but still cause bestrophinopathy.
source: We recently identified several gain-of-function mutations, which enhance the channel activity when transiently expressed in HEK293 cells but still cause bestrophinopathy (Ji et al., 2019a), suggesting the physiological importance of maintaining normal BEST1 functionality.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ji et al., 2019a).

claim: Allelic expression imbalance at the BEST1 locus has been observed in human RPE.
source: This is essential for evaluating the pathogenicity of different BEST1 mutations, especially considering that allelic expression imbalance (AEI) at the BEST1 locus has been observed in human RPE (Llavona et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Llavona et al., 2017).

claim: All six autosomal dominant loss-of-function BEST1 mutations behaved recessively at a 1:1 ratio with WT BEST1.
source: Strikingly, all six autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations behaved recessively at a 1:1 ratio with the WT BEST1 and required a superior 4:1 ratio to exhibit the mutant phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Six autosomal dominant loss-of-function BEST1 mutations required a 4:1 ratio with WT BEST1 to exhibit the mutant phenotype.
source: Strikingly, all six autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations behaved recessively at a 1:1 ratio with the WT BEST1 and required a superior 4:1 ratio to exhibit the mutant phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Six autosomal dominant loss-of-function BEST1 mutations act in a dominant-negative manner rather than the canonical dominant manner.
source: It suggests that they act in a dominant-negative manner rather than the canonical dominant manner, which explains our previous results that gene augmentation is sufficient for the rescue of autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations (Ji et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing recessive behavior at 1:1 ratio and dominant-negative behavior at 4:1 ratio.

claim: The mutant BEST1 allele is transcribed at a higher level than the WT allele in patient-derived RPE cells.
source: Consistent with this finding, the mutant BEST1 allele is transcribed at a higher level than the WT allele in patient-derived RPE cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: All three autosomal dominant gain-of-function BEST1 mutations displayed dominant behavior even at an inferior 1:4 ratio with WT BEST1.
source: In sharp contrast, all three autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutations displayed a dominant behavior, even at an inferior 1:4 ratio with the WT BEST1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: BEST1 gain-of-function mutations cannot be rescued by gene augmentation alone.
source: Due to their strong dominant effect, BEST1 gain-of-function mutations cannot be rescued by gene augmentation alone, but require CRISPR/Cas9-mediated silencing of the endogenous BEST1 in combination with gene augmentation for restoring Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in RPE cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: BEST1 gain-of-function mutations require CRISPR/Cas9-mediated silencing of endogenous BEST1 in combination with gene augmentation for restoring Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in RPE cells.
source: Due to their strong dominant effect, BEST1 gain-of-function mutations cannot be rescued by gene augmentation alone, but require CRISPR/Cas9-mediated silencing of the endogenous BEST1 in combination with gene augmentation for restoring Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in RPE cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: BEST1 is the bona fide CaCC in RPE.
source: Additionally, we confirmed the physiological role of BEST1 as the bona fide CaCC in RPE.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing abolished currents in BEST1-/- cells but not in TMEM16A-/-, TMEM16B-/-, or LRRC8A-/- cells.

claim: Cl- currents from cells co-expressing mutant and WT BEST1 at 1:1 ratio were similar to those from cells expressing WT BEST1 alone for six autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations.
source: Surprisingly, in the presence of 1.2 μM free intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i), where BEST1 conducts peak current (Li et al., 2017), Cl- currents from cells co-expressing mutant and WT BEST1 were similar to those from cells expressing WT BEST1 alone (Figure 1a–h cyan, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), regardless of whether the mutation is autosomal dominant or recessive.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Six loss-of-function BEST1 mutations, although genetically defined as autosomal dominant, do not exhibit dominant behavior in vitro at 1:1 ratio with WT.
source: Therefore, these six loss-of-function mutations, although genetically defined as autosomal dominant, do not exhibit dominant behavior in vitro.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing similar currents to WT at 1:1 ratio.

claim: At 4:1 mutant to WT ratio, Cl- currents from co-expression of an autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutant and WT BEST1 were significantly smaller than those from WT only.
source: At 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i, Cl- currents from co-expression of an autosomal dominant mutant and WT BEST1 were significantly smaller than those from the WT only, and similar to those from the mutant only (Figure 1b–g magenta, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Currents from cells co-expressing the autosomal recessive P274R mutant and WT BEST1 at 4:1 ratio were similar to those from cells expressing WT BEST1 only.
source: By contrast, currents from cells co-expressing the autosomal recessive P274R mutant and the WT BEST1 at a 4:1 ratio were still similar to those from cells expressing the WT BEST1 only (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The six previously recognized autosomal dominant BEST1 mutations are actually dominant-negative in vitro.
source: Therefore, the six previously recognized autosomal dominant mutations are actually dominant-negative in vitro, whereas the autosomal recessive P274R mutation indeed behaves recessively.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing recessive behavior at 1:1 and dominant-negative behavior at 4:1.

claim: The autosomal recessive P274R mutation behaves recessively in vitro.
source: Therefore, the six previously recognized autosomal dominant mutations are actually dominant-negative in vitro, whereas the autosomal recessive P274R mutation indeed behaves recessively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing WT-like currents at both 1:1 and 4:1 ratios.

claim: The mutant BEST1 genotype showed up three to four times more than the WT in all 12 BVMD patient-derived iPSC-RPE clones.
source: Remarkably, the mutant genotype showed up three to four times more than the WT in all 12 BVMD patient-derived iPSC-RPE clones (two clones from each patient) (Table 1), indicating that the transcription level of the mutant allele is three- to fourfold higher than that of the WT allele in these patients' RPE cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The transcription level of the mutant BEST1 allele is three- to fourfold higher than that of the WT allele in patient RPE cells.
source: Remarkably, the mutant genotype showed up three to four times more than the WT in all 12 BVMD patient-derived iPSC-RPE clones (two clones from each patient) (Table 1), indicating that the transcription level of the mutant allele is three- to fourfold higher than that of the WT allele in these patients' RPE cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing 3-4 fold more mutant transcripts in Table 1.

claim: Transcripts from one BEST1 allele outnumbered those from the other by approximately threefold in native human RPE cells from a donor with an SNP.
source: Consistent with results from iPSC-RPE, transcripts from one allele outnumbered those from the other by approximately threefold in these native human RPE cells (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Allelic imbalance of BEST1 transcription contributes to the dominant-negative effect of autosomal dominant mutations.
source: Together, our results suggest that allelic imbalance of BEST1 transcription contributes to the dominant-negative effect of the autosomal dominant mutations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing higher mutant allele transcription and dominant-negative behavior at 4:1 ratio.

claim: Gene augmentation can restore Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in iPSC-RPE cells bearing a BEST1 autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutation when augmented WT BEST1 protein is expressed at a similar or higher level compared to endogenous BEST1.
source: Importantly, this provides an explanation for the restoration of Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents by gene augmentation in iPSC-RPE cells bearing a BEST1 autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutation (Ji et al., 2019b): as long as the augmented WT BEST1 protein is expressed at a similar or higher level compared to the endogenous BEST1, the mutant to WT protein ratio is no longer in a dominant-negative scenario, such that the WT phenotype is exhibited as seen in 1:1 transiently transfected HEK293 cells (Figure 1b–g).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data and cited prior work (Ji et al., 2019b).

claim: Three BEST1 gain-of-function mutations (D203A, I205T, and Y236C) are all autosomal dominant.
source: We previously identified three BEST1 gain-of-function mutations, namely D203A, I205T, and Y236C, all of which are autosomal dominant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Ji et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ji et al., 2019a).

claim: At 1:1 ratio with WT BEST1, cells co-expressing WT and any of the three gain-of-function mutants showed significantly larger Cl- currents than WT only in the absence of Ca2+.
source: Without Ca2+, Cl- currents from cells co-expressing WT BEST1 and any of the mutants were significantly larger than those from cells expressing WT BEST1 only; at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i, cells co-expressing D203A/WT and Y236C/WT displayed significantly bigger currents than WT only (Figure 2a–c left, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a); at both conditions, currents from cells co-expressing mutant/WT BEST1 resembled those from cells expressing the mutant only (Figure 2a–c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: At 1.2 μM Ca2+, cells co-expressing D203A/WT and Y236C/WT displayed significantly bigger currents than WT only.
source: Without Ca2+, Cl- currents from cells co-expressing WT BEST1 and any of the mutants were significantly larger than those from cells expressing WT BEST1 only; at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i, cells co-expressing D203A/WT and Y236C/WT displayed significantly bigger currents than WT only (Figure 2a–c left, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a); at both conditions, currents from cells co-expressing mutant/WT BEST1 resembled those from cells expressing the mutant only (Figure 2a–c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Currents from cells co-expressing gain-of-function mutant/WT BEST1 at 1:1 ratio resembled those from cells expressing the mutant only.
source: Without Ca2+, Cl- currents from cells co-expressing WT BEST1 and any of the mutants were significantly larger than those from cells expressing WT BEST1 only; at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i, cells co-expressing D203A/WT and Y236C/WT displayed significantly bigger currents than WT only (Figure 2a–c left, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a); at both conditions, currents from cells co-expressing mutant/WT BEST1 resembled those from cells expressing the mutant only (Figure 2a–c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Three BEST1 gain-of-function mutations are indeed dominant, in contrast to the dominant-negative behavior of six loss-of-function mutations.
source: These results indicate that these three gain-of-function mutations are indeed dominant, in contrast to the dominant-negative behavior of the six loss-of-function mutations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data comparing gain-of-function and loss-of-function mutations.

claim: At 1:4 mutant to WT ratio, Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents from co-expression of a gain-of-function mutant and WT BEST1 were similar to those from the mutant only.
source: Under this condition, Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents from co-expression of a gain-of-function mutant and WT BEST1 were still similar to those from the mutant only (Figure 2a–c right, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Just one gain-of-function mutant monomer is sufficient to dominate the function of the pentameric BEST1 channel.
source: These results suggest a potent dominant effect of the gain-of-function mutations: just one mutant monomer is sufficient to dominate the function of the pentameric channel.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing dominant effect at 1:4 ratio.

claim: All three gain-of-function mutants were expressed at similar levels to that of WT BEST1 after transient transfection.
source: All three gain-of-function mutants were expressed at similar levels to that of WT BEST1 after transient transfection, and retained the interaction with WT BEST1 (Figure 2d), consistent with our previous observation that the interaction between BEST1 monomers is not affected by loss-of-function autosomal dominant mutations (Ji et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Gain-of-function BEST1 mutants retained the interaction with WT BEST1.
source: All three gain-of-function mutants were expressed at similar levels to that of WT BEST1 after transient transfection, and retained the interaction with WT BEST1 (Figure 2d), consistent with our previous observation that the interaction between BEST1 monomers is not affected by loss-of-function autosomal dominant mutations (Ji et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The interaction between BEST1 monomers is not affected by loss-of-function autosomal dominant mutations.
source: All three gain-of-function mutants were expressed at similar levels to that of WT BEST1 after transient transfection, and retained the interaction with WT BEST1 (Figure 2d), consistent with our previous observation that the interaction between BEST1 monomers is not affected by loss-of-function autosomal dominant mutations (Ji et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ji et al., 2019b).

claim: WT gene augmentation is sufficient to restore Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in iPSC-RPE cells with a BEST1 loss-of-function mutation while exogenous BEST1 is expressed at a comparable level to endogenous protein.
source: We previously showed that WT gene augmentation is sufficient to restore Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in iPSC-RPE cells with a BEST1 loss-of-function mutation, while the exogenous BEST1 is expressed at a comparable level to the endogenous protein (Ji et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ji et al., 2019b).

claim: Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents on the plasma membrane of BEST1WT/WT hPSC-RPE cells were recorded as 4 ± 1 and 267 ± 79 pA/pF at 0 and 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i, respectively.
source: Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents on the plasma membrane of BEST1WT/WT hPSC-RPE cells were recorded as 4 ± 1 and 267 ± 79 pA/pF at 0 and 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i, respectively, consistent with results from donor-derived BEST1WT/WT iPSC-RPE (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in BEST1WT/WT hPSC-RPE are consistent with results from donor-derived BEST1WT/WT iPSC-RPE.
source: Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents on the plasma membrane of BEST1WT/WT hPSC-RPE cells were recorded as 4 ± 1 and 267 ± 79 pA/pF at 0 and 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i, respectively, consistent with results from donor-derived BEST1WT/WT iPSC-RPE (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Only the mRNA of BEST1, but not of TMEM16A, TMEM16B, or LRRC8A, can be detected in WT PSC-RPE or donor native RPE cells.
source: It should be noted that only the mRNA of BEST1, but not of the other three CaCCs, can be detected in WT PSC-RPE or donor native RPE cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–b.

claim: Ca2+-dependent Cl- current was completely eliminated in BEST1-/- hPSC-RPE and a patient-derived BEST1 null iPSC-RPE.
source: Remarkably, Ca2+-dependent Cl- current was completely eliminated in BEST1-/- hPSC-RPE and a patient-derived BEST1 null (IVS1 +5G>A homo) iPSC-RPE (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–d; Fung et al., 2015), in contrast to the WT-like currents from TMEM16A-/-, TMEM16B-/-, or LRRC8A-/- hPSC-RPE cells (Figure 3c–e, Figure 3—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: TMEM16A-/-, TMEM16B-/-, or LRRC8A-/- hPSC-RPE cells showed WT-like Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents.
source: Remarkably, Ca2+-dependent Cl- current was completely eliminated in BEST1-/- hPSC-RPE and a patient-derived BEST1 null (IVS1 +5G>A homo) iPSC-RPE (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–d; Fung et al., 2015), in contrast to the WT-like currents from TMEM16A-/-, TMEM16B-/-, or LRRC8A-/- hPSC-RPE cells (Figure 3c–e, Figure 3—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c–e and Figure 3—figure supplement 3d.

claim: The protein and mRNA levels of BEST1 were abolished in BEST1-/- hPSC-RPE cells.
source: Consistently, the protein and mRNA levels of BEST1 were abolished in BEST1-/- hPSC-RPE cells, but not affected in TMEM16A-/-, TMEM16B-/-, or LRRC8A-/- hPSC-RPE cells (Figure 3—figure supplements 1a and 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1a and 2c.

claim: The protein and mRNA levels of BEST1 were not affected in TMEM16A-/-, TMEM16B-/-, or LRRC8A-/- hPSC-RPE cells.
source: Consistently, the protein and mRNA levels of BEST1 were abolished in BEST1-/- hPSC-RPE cells, but not affected in TMEM16A-/-, TMEM16B-/-, or LRRC8A-/- hPSC-RPE cells (Figure 3—figure supplements 1a and 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1a and 2c.

claim: When WT BEST1 was expressed from a baculovirus vector in BEST1-/- hPSC-RPE and patient-derived BEST1 null iPSC-RPE, Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents were fully rescued.
source: Moreover, when WT BEST1 was expressed from a baculovirus vector in BEST1-/- hPSC-RPE and the patient-derived BEST1 null iPSC-RPE, Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents were fully rescued (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 3c.

claim: hPSC-RPE is a valid model system to study BEST1 function.
source: Taken together, these results validate hPSC-RPE as a model system to study BEST1 function, and indicate that BEST1, but not TMEM16A, TMEM16B, or LRRC8A, is the CaCC conducting Ca2+-dependent Cl- current in human RPE.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing similar currents in hPSC-RPE and iPSC-RPE.

claim: BEST1, but not TMEM16A, TMEM16B, or LRRC8A, is the CaCC conducting Ca2+-dependent Cl- current in human RPE.
source: Taken together, these results validate hPSC-RPE as a model system to study BEST1 function, and indicate that BEST1, but not TMEM16A, TMEM16B, or LRRC8A, is the CaCC conducting Ca2+-dependent Cl- current in human RPE.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing abolished currents only in BEST1-/- cells.

claim: Cl- currents from BEST1I205T/WT hPSC-RPE were significantly bigger than those from WT under no or low Ca2+ conditions.
source: Consistent with results from transiently transfected HEK293 cells (Ji et al., 2019a), Cl- currents from BEST1I205T/WT hPSC-RPE were significantly bigger than those from WT under no or low Ca2+ conditions, but similar in the presence of high Ca2+ (Figure 4a–c, Figure 3—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a–c and Figure 3—figure supplement 3d.

claim: Cl- currents from BEST1I205T/WT hPSC-RPE were similar to WT in the presence of high Ca2+.
source: Consistent with results from transiently transfected HEK293 cells (Ji et al., 2019a), Cl- currents from BEST1I205T/WT hPSC-RPE were significantly bigger than those from WT under no or low Ca2+ conditions, but similar in the presence of high Ca2+ (Figure 4a–c, Figure 3—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a–c and Figure 3—figure supplement 3d.

claim: Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents from BEST1Y236C/WT hPSC-RPE were significantly larger than those from WT at all tested [Ca2+]i.
source: On the other hand, the Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents from BEST1Y236C/WT hPSC-RPE were significantly larger than those from WT at all tested [Ca2+]is (Figure 4d–f, Figure 3—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d–f and Figure 3—figure supplement 3d.

claim: The results reaffirm the gain-of-function and dominant behavior of the BEST1 I205T and Y236C mutations in RPE.
source: These results reaffirm the gain-of-function and dominant behavior of the BEST1 I205T and Y236C mutations in RPE.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in hPSC-RPE cells.

claim: Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in BEST1I205T/WT and BEST1Y236C/WT hPSC-RPE cells remained aberrant after gene augmentation in the absence of Ca2+.
source: Notably, Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in these mutant hPSC-RPE cells remained aberrant after gene augmentation in the absence of Ca2+ (Figure 4b and e, open blue), despite the exogenous WT BEST1 being expressed at a higher level to that of the endogenous BEST1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b, 4e, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Gene augmentation alone is insufficient to rescue BEST1 gain-of-function mutations.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that gene augmentation alone is insufficient to rescue BEST1 gain-of-function mutations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing persistent aberrant currents after gene augmentation.

claim: BVSi 3–8 virus showed better BEST1 knockdown efficiency compared to BVSi 5–4 virus.
source: Immunoblotting showed a better BEST1 knockdown efficiency of the BVSi 3–8 virus compared to the BVSi 5–4 virus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Ca2+-dependent Cl- current from BVSi 3–8 infected cells was more effectively diminished compared to that from BVSi 5–4 infected cells at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i.
source: Consistently, Ca2+-dependent Cl- current from BVSi 3–8 infected cells was more effectively diminished compared to that from BVSi 5–4 infected cells at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i (Figure 5a), where RPE cells display the peak Cl- current amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The diminished Ca2+-dependent Cl- current in BVSi 3–8 treated WT hPSC-RPE cells was fully rescued when wobble WT BEST1-mCherry was co-expressed at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i.
source: When wobble WT BEST1-mCherry was co-expressed, the diminished Ca2+-dependent Cl- current in BVSi 3–8 treated WT hPSC-RPE cells was fully rescued at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i (Figure 5b), validating our silencing/augmentation system in WT hPSC-RPE cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The endogenous BEST1 protein was diminished with BVSi 3–8 treatment in BEST1I205T/WT and BEST1Y236C/WT hPSC-RPE cells.
source: Remarkably, the endogenous BEST1 protein was diminished with BVSi 3–8 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) in the mutant hPSC-RPE cells, concomitant with abolished Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in these cells at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i (Figure 5c–d), while co-expression of the wobble WT BEST1-mCherry restored Cl- currents to the WT levels at all tested [Ca2+]is (Figure 5c–f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), providing a proof-of-concept for the cure of bestrophinopathies associated with BEST1 gain-of-function mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents were abolished in BEST1I205T/WT and BEST1Y236C/WT hPSC-RPE cells at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i after BVSi 3–8 treatment.
source: Remarkably, the endogenous BEST1 protein was diminished with BVSi 3–8 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) in the mutant hPSC-RPE cells, concomitant with abolished Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in these cells at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i (Figure 5c–d), while co-expression of the wobble WT BEST1-mCherry restored Cl- currents to the WT levels at all tested [Ca2+]is (Figure 5c–f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), providing a proof-of-concept for the cure of bestrophinopathies associated with BEST1 gain-of-function mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c–d.

claim: Co-expression of wobble WT BEST1-mCherry restored Cl- currents to WT levels at all tested [Ca2+]i in BEST1I205T/WT and BEST1Y236C/WT hPSC-RPE cells treated with BVSi 3–8.
source: Remarkably, the endogenous BEST1 protein was diminished with BVSi 3–8 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) in the mutant hPSC-RPE cells, concomitant with abolished Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in these cells at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i (Figure 5c–d), while co-expression of the wobble WT BEST1-mCherry restored Cl- currents to the WT levels at all tested [Ca2+]is (Figure 5c–f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), providing a proof-of-concept for the cure of bestrophinopathies associated with BEST1 gain-of-function mutations.

claim: The silencing plus augmentation strategy provides a proof-of-concept for the cure of bestrophinopathies associated with BEST1 gain-of-function mutations.
source: Remarkably, the endogenous BEST1 protein was diminished with BVSi 3–8 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) in the mutant hPSC-RPE cells, concomitant with abolished Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents in these cells at 1.2 μM [Ca2+]i (Figure 5c–d), while co-expression of the wobble WT BEST1-mCherry restored Cl- currents to the WT levels at all tested [Ca2+]is (Figure 5c–f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), providing a proof-of-concept for the cure of bestrophinopathies associated with BEST1 gain-of-function mutations.

claim: Autosomal dominant loss-of-function BEST1 mutations only dominated over WT BEST1 at a superior 4:1 ratio, but not at a canonical 1:1 ratio.
source: Although the recessive and gain-of-function mutations indeed exhibited their expected recessive and dominant behaviors, respectively, the autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations only dominated over the WT BEST1 at a superior 4:1 ratio, but not at a canonical 1:1 ratio (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The majority of the over 250 documented BEST1 disease-causing mutations are autosomal dominant and display loss-of-function when tested in vitro.
source: As the majority of the over 250 documented BEST1 disease-causing mutations are autosomal dominant and display loss-of-function when tested in vitro, our results indicate an important role of allele-specific epigenetic control in the development of bestrophinopathies.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Allele-specific epigenetic control plays an important role in the development of bestrophinopathies.
source: As the majority of the over 250 documented BEST1 disease-causing mutations are autosomal dominant and display loss-of-function when tested in vitro, our results indicate an important role of allele-specific epigenetic control in the development of bestrophinopathies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing allelic imbalance and dominant-negative behavior.

claim: Imbalanced transcription of the two endogenous BEST1 alleles was detected in donor-derived iPSC-RPE and native RPE cells.
source: In strong support of this finding, imbalanced transcription of the two endogenous BEST1 alleles was detected in donor-derived iPSC-RPE and native RPE cells (Table 1), consistent with the previous observation that BEST1 is one of the inherited retinal disease genes with AEI in the human retinal transcriptome (Llavona et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: BEST1 is one of the inherited retinal disease genes with AEI in the human retinal transcriptome.
source: In strong support of this finding, imbalanced transcription of the two endogenous BEST1 alleles was detected in donor-derived iPSC-RPE and native RPE cells (Table 1), consistent with the previous observation that BEST1 is one of the inherited retinal disease genes with AEI in the human retinal transcriptome (Llavona et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Llavona et al., 2017).

claim: More than half of 602 surveyed human genes display AEI.
source: An SNP array-based survey of 602 human genes discovered that more than half of the genes display AEI (Lo et al., 2003), while a separate study analyzing the mouse transcriptome revealed that ~20% of genes are prone to AEI in a tissue-specific manner (Pinter et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Lo et al., 2003).

claim: Approximately 20% of mouse genes are prone to AEI in a tissue-specific manner.
source: An SNP array-based survey of 602 human genes discovered that more than half of the genes display AEI (Lo et al., 2003), while a separate study analyzing the mouse transcriptome revealed that ~20% of genes are prone to AEI in a tissue-specific manner (Pinter et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Pinter et al., 2015).

claim: AEI of somatic mutations has been well documented in the context of cancer.
source: Moreover, AEI of somatic mutations has been well documented in the context of cancer (Bielski et al., 2018; Rhee et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2002a; Bielski and Taylor, 2021), representing an important mechanism of tumorigenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bestrophinopathies caused by autosomal dominant mutations of BEST1 may serve as a paradigm to address the influence of AEI in Mendelian disorders.
source: To our knowledge, the linkage between an inherited missense mutation and AEI in pathogenesis has not been established yet. Our results suggest that bestrophinopathies caused by autosomal dominant mutations of BEST1 may serve as a paradigm to address the influence of AEI in Mendelian disorders.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the novel findings in this study.

claim: A portion of bestrophinopathy-causing mutations previously classified as autosomal dominant are de facto recessive and exhibit a dominant-negative phenotype when their expression outweighs that of the WT allele in vivo.
source: Therefore, we anticipate that a portion of the bestrophinopathy-causing mutations previously classified as autosomal dominant are de facto recessive and exhibit a dominant-negative phenotype when their expression outweighs that of the WT allele in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing recessive behavior at 1:1 and dominant-negative at 4:1.

claim: Gene augmentation is sufficient to rescue BEST1 loss-of-function mutations regardless of their inheritance patterns.
source: This is in line with our previous finding that gene augmentation is sufficient to rescue BEST1 loss-of-function mutations regardless of their inheritance patterns (Ji et al., 2019b), and provides an explanation for incomplete penetrance and variable clinical expressivity in patients bearing the same BEST1 mutations (Sodi et al., 2012; Cohn et al., 2011; Arora et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ji et al., 2019b).

claim: The findings provide an explanation for incomplete penetrance and variable clinical expressivity in patients bearing the same BEST1 mutations.
source: This is in line with our previous finding that gene augmentation is sufficient to rescue BEST1 loss-of-function mutations regardless of their inheritance patterns (Ji et al., 2019b), and provides an explanation for incomplete penetrance and variable clinical expressivity in patients bearing the same BEST1 mutations (Sodi et al., 2012; Cohn et al., 2011; Arora et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the findings and supported by citations.

claim: TMEM16A and TMEM16B have been proposed to be physiological CaCC(s) in porcine or mouse RPE and human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells.
source: However, other candidates, including TMEM16A and TMEM16B, have also been proposed to be the physiological CaCC(s) in porcine or mouse RPE and the human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells (Schreiber and Kunzelmann, 2016; Keckeis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents were diminished in BEST1-/- cells and remained intact in TMEM16A-/-, TMEM16B-/-, or LRRC8A-/- cells.
source: Our results from isogenic knockout hPSC-RPE cells showed that Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents were diminished in BEST1-/- cells, and remained intact in TMEM16A-/-, TMEM16B-/-, or LRRC8A-/- cells (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Almost identical Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents were recorded from BEST1WT/WT hPSC-RPE compared to those from BEST1WT/WT iPSC-RPE.
source: Importantly, almost identical Ca2+-dependent Cl- currents were recorded from BEST1WT/WT hPSC-RPE compared to those from BEST1WT/WT iPSC-RPE (Figure 3a), validating hPSC-RPE as a versatile tool to model BEST1 mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: ARB is specifically caused by BEST1 autosomal recessive mutations, which require five mutant protomers in a channel pentamer to be phenotypic.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, ARB is specifically caused by BEST1 autosomal recessive mutations, which represent the 'weakest' class that requires five mutant protomers in a channel pentamer to be phenotypic (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data and knowledge of ARB.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations such as D203A, I205T, and Y236C represent the 'strongest' class, which predominates over WT BEST1 even at a 1:4 ratio (presumably one protomer per channel).
source: On the other hand, gain-of-function mutations such as D203A, I205T, and Y236C represent the 'strongest' class, which predominates over the WT BEST1 even at a 1:4 ratio (presumably one protomer per channel, Figure 2a–c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), although it remains unclear if they are specifically linked to a certain type of bestrophinopathy.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations likely represent 'intermediate' classes, which require 2–4 protomers in a BEST1 channel to display the mutant phenotype.
source: Autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations likely represent the 'intermediate' classes, which require 2–4 protomers in a BEST1 channel to display the mutant phenotype.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from experimental data.

claim: The six loss-of-function mutations tested (A10T, R218H, L234P, A243T, Q293K, and D302A) may represent the 4-mutant-protomer class as they are only dominant-negative at a 4:1 ratio with WT in HEK293 cells.
source: For instance, the six loss-of-function mutations tested in this study (A10T, R218H, L234P, A243T, Q293K, and D302A) may represent the 4-mutant-protomer class as they are only dominant-negative at a 4:1 ratio with the WT in HEK293 cells, while Y85H, R92C, R218S, and G299E may represent the 2/3-mutant-protomer class(es), as they were previously shown to be dominant over the WT at a 1:1 ratio in HEK293 cells (Sun et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in this study.

claim: Y85H, R92C, R218S, and G299E may represent the 2/3-mutant-protomer class(es), as they were previously shown to be dominant over WT at a 1:1 ratio in HEK293 cells.
source: For instance, the six loss-of-function mutations tested in this study (A10T, R218H, L234P, A243T, Q293K, and D302A) may represent the 4-mutant-protomer class as they are only dominant-negative at a 4:1 ratio with the WT in HEK293 cells, while Y85H, R92C, R218S, and G299E may represent the 2/3-mutant-protomer class(es), as they were previously shown to be dominant over the WT at a 1:1 ratio in HEK293 cells (Sun et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sun et al., 2002).

claim: All three BEST1 gain-of-function mutations exhibit a strong dominant effect, suppressing WT even at a 1:4 ratio.
source: All three BEST1 gain-of-function mutations in this study exhibit a strong dominant effect, suppressing the WT even at a 1:4 ratio (Figure 2a–c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: For effective gene augmentation therapy of gain-of-function mutations, the total level of WT BEST1 protein must be at least four folds higher than that of the endogenous mutant BEST1.
source: This suggests that for effective gene augmentation therapy, the total level of WT BEST1 protein, supplied both endogenously and exogenously, must be at least four folds higher than that of the endogenous mutant BEST1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing dominant effect at 1:4 ratio.

claim: Even with a CMV promoter producing a higher level of exogenous BEST1 protein compared to endogenous BEST1, the gain-of-function phenotype in BEST1I205T/WT and BEST1Y236C/WT hPSC-RPE cells cannot be rescued.
source: However, we showed that even with a CMV promoter, which produces an apparently higher level of exogenous BEST1 protein compared to that of endogenous BEST1, the gain-of-function phenotype in BEST1I205T/WT and BEST1Y236C/WT hPSC-RPE cells cannot be rescued (Figure 4b and e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: It is impractical to rescue BEST1 gain-of-function mutations by gene augmentation alone.
source: Therefore, it seems impractical to rescue BEST1 gain-of-function mutations by gene augmentation alone, especially considering that clinical applications may require the use of the native BEST1 promotor, which is presumably not as strong as the CMV promotor.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data and practical considerations.

claim: The three gain-of-function mutations (D203A, I205T, and Y236C) are located at or in close proximity to the neck or aperture of the BEST1 channel.
source: Structurally, the three gain-of-function mutations (D203A, I205T, and Y236C) are located at or in a close proximity to the neck (I76, F80, and F84) or the aperture (I205) of the channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and are involved in the opening of at least one of these two Ca2+-dependent gates (Ji et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations.

claim: The three gain-of-function mutations are involved in the opening of at least one of the two Ca2+-dependent gates.
source: Structurally, the three gain-of-function mutations (D203A, I205T, and Y236C) are located at or in a close proximity to the neck (I76, F80, and F84) or the aperture (I205) of the channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and are involved in the opening of at least one of these two Ca2+-dependent gates (Ji et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The I205T mutation causes a Ca2+-independent 'leak' due to enlargement of the channel constriction.
source: For instance, the I205T mutation, replacing a bulky isoleucine with a smaller side-chained threonine at the aperture (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), causes a Ca2+-independent "leak" due to enlargement of the channel constriction (Figure 2b, Figure 4a-c; Ji et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: Loss-of-function BEST1 mutations are located in various regions of the channel.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ji et al., 2019b).

claim: The BEST1 genomic locus recognized by the BVSi design does not have any reported disease-causing mutations or polymorphisms.
source: As the BEST1 genomic locus recognized by our BVSi does not have any reported disease-causing mutations or polymorphisms, this BVSi design is universally suited for BEST1 silencing in bestrophinopathy patients no matter where their mutations are located within the gene.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of reported mutations.

claim: The BVSi design is universally suited for BEST1 silencing in bestrophinopathy patients regardless of mutation location.
source: As the BEST1 genomic locus recognized by our BVSi does not have any reported disease-causing mutations or polymorphisms, this BVSi design is universally suited for BEST1 silencing in bestrophinopathy patients no matter where their mutations are located within the gene.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the design of the BVSi system.

claim: Simultaneously suppressing endogenous BEST1 does not interfere with functional restoration by gene augmentation for loss-of-function mutations.
source: Notably, although gene augmentation alone is readily sufficient to rescue loss-of-function mutations (Ji et al., 2019b), simultaneously suppressing the endogenous BEST1 does not interfere with the functional restoration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental results.

claim: The silencing plus augmentation combination strategy can potentially be utilized for the treatment of all bestrophinopathies.
source: Therefore, our silencing plus augmentation combination strategy can potentially be utilized for the treatment of all bestrophinopathies.
